When the market is ripping you have to accept that the "clean" high time frame retests you want may never come.  

If they do happen, it's usually after price has already extended significantly to the upside. 

There will still be spots where we get large corrections but they are few and far between and require patience and a belief in your bias not to get bearish during them.

Active trading should be focused on lower timeframes and you need to stop assuming every move is going to immediately mean revert as in prior price regimes. 

Lastly, you need to decide if you are willing to buy things that have already broken out with momentum and risk buying a top before a pullback or wait for those high time frame retest and risk being sidelined.

NEAR is building the infrastructure for AI agents to hire one another.

Most agent commerce today is built around fixed services that can be priced per call. Hiring another agent creates a different kind of transaction because the buyer is paying for an outcome that may take several steps to produce. NEAR is building a single stack around the full process.

Agent Market turns a task and budget into an open job that agents can bid on. The selected provider executes the work and is paid through escrow. Delivery can run through IronClaw with private inference supplied by NEAR AI Cloud. NEAR Intents supports settlement.

Completing the transaction requires one more step: deciding whether the provider delivered what was promised. That becomes difficult when the work requires expertise the requester does not have.

With reliable verification, the model NEAR is building could take agentic commerce beyond pay-per-call services and into markets for completed work.

Most agent commerce today is built around fixed services that can be priced per call. Hiring another agent creates a different kind of transaction because the buyer is paying for an outcome that may take several steps to produce. NEAR is building a single stack around the full process.

Agent Market turns a task and budget into an open job that agents can bid on. The selected provider executes the work and is paid through escrow. Delivery can run through IronClaw with private inference supplied by NEAR AI Cloud. NEAR Intents supports settlement.

Completing the transaction requires one more step: deciding whether the provider delivered what was promised. That becomes difficult when the work requires expertise the requester does not have.

With reliable verification, the model NEAR is building could take agentic commerce beyond pay-per-call services and into markets for completed work.

That is the asymmetry: Rush investors are effectively paying only for the Myriad shares while receiving a potentially significant niobium-uranium exploration asset for free.

My read is that this may seem like a compelling narrative, but there are so many exaggerations and logical leaps strung together to get there, that I find the conclusion pretty unlikely.

Take the claim that 35–40% of hyperscaler capex is going to memory. Bottom-up, I get closer to 20–25% (SemiAnalysis estimates 30%). And even that is a snapshot of a brutal shortage after the memory makers spent the 2022–24 downturn slashing production and capex.

Micro and Hynix are currently earning ~80% operating margins. I would not treat their one (admittedly huge) component of the AI stack as a permanently scarce input. New supply is being funded via SLAs, and not at these economics. Also, industry DRAM and NAND bit supply is already growing ~20% this year, quite contrary to his claim that memory makers are simply shipping "the same amount at higher prices." These little mistatements add up. I think he uses them to make overly provocative conclusions.

There are similar problems throughout. Like his fact that 60% of announced 2027 projects haven't broken ground. Mostly tells me some projects are late, not that capex "is NOT creating more data centers." 10 GW of new U.S. capacity finished through 1H26 says otherwise.

(I also don't necessarily agree that moving workloads from expensive frontier models to cheaper ones is demand destruction. Lowering the cost per task could just as easily increase total AI usage.)

You can follow the breadcrumbs from there.

For me, full disclosure, rather than try to time an exit and re-entry from these levels, unless something changes in the fundamentals, I'll probably just keep consolidating into my favorite names and buying them lower. Thats what the diversification was there for.

Real connection lives in inconvenience.

A few months ago I sat down with @PeterDiamandis  and @salimismail on The Journeyman and we got into this. 

Salim made a brilliant point... in the nineties we introduced video calls so nobody would ever have to travel again. Yet the conference industry has never been bigger. We still get on the plane, sit in traffic and stand around hotel lobbies. Why? because community is worth the inconvenience. Putting yourself out for other people is exactly what makes it mean something.

We've spent decades optimising for a hyper-convenient life. And the machines will finish the job... they'll be able to do everything convenient. The one thing they can't do is show up. Be in the room. Be there.

That's why Im not worried about whats coming. The things that make us human are about to become the most valuable things we have.
